To elope means to secretly run away with the person you love in order to get married — typically without telling your parents or family, and often without their approval.

Imagine a couple who want to get married, but their parents strongly disapprove of the relationship. Instead of fighting with the family or waiting for permission, the couple quietly slips away — perhaps to another city or even another country — gets married there, and only tells everyone afterward. That is eloping.

The act of eloping has three essential ingredients:

1. Secrecy. This is the most defining feature. The couple does not announce their plans. They keep it hidden, at least until after the marriage has taken place. The family usually finds out only once it is already done.

2. Running away. There is a sense of leaving — escaping your usual surroundings. The couple goes somewhere else to get married, away from the people who might try to stop them.

3. Marriage. This is critical. Eloping is specifically and exclusively about getting married. You would never use this word for running away for any other reason. If someone says "they eloped," it means they got married, not that they simply fled somewhere together.

The most classic reason is family opposition — parents who disapprove of the partner because of religion, culture, social class, age, or simply personal dislike. Rather than fight that battle, the couple takes matters into their own hands.

Other reasons include:

  • Wanting to avoid the stress, cost, and drama of a big wedding
  • Desiring something deeply personal and intimate — just the two of them
  • Simply being impulsive and swept up in the moment
How the word is used grammatically

"Elope" is almost always paired with the preposition with:

  • She eloped with her boyfriend.
  • They decided to elope with each other.

You do not "elope someone" — you "elope with someone."

Past tense: eloped
Noun form: elopement (the act of eloping)

• "Her parents were furious when they discovered she had eloped." — The marriage had already happened before they found out.
  • "He always dreamed of eloping to Paris." — Running away to another place to get married privately.
  • "Instead of planning a big wedding, they chose to elope." — Opting for secrecy and simplicity over a formal celebration.
  • "The elopement shocked the whole family." — Using the noun form.
  • "They had been secretly planning to elope for months." — Showing the premeditated, hidden nature of it.
The "feel" of the word — its connotations

"Elope" carries a distinctly romantic, almost cinematic quality. It suggests a love powerful enough to defy family opposition or social convention. When you hear someone eloped, you tend to picture two people driven by deep feeling rather than careful planning — a kind of passionate, rebellious act.

At the same time, depending on the context, it can also carry a slightly negative or scandalous undertone — suggesting the couple acted rashly, that they had something to hide, or that they showed disrespect to family by excluding them from such a major life event. The word can be used admiringly ("How romantic — they just eloped!") or disapprovingly ("They eloped without even telling her mother"), depending entirely on the speaker's perspective.

Traditionally, eloping always involved secrecy and running away. In modern usage, however, the word has softened somewhat. Today, many people use "elope" to mean simply getting married in a very small, private ceremony — just the two of them, or with one or two witnesses — even if the family is informed beforehand and no one is truly "running away."

So you might hear someone say, "We didn't want a big wedding, so we eloped," when in fact their family knew about it. This looser usage is now very common, especially in casual conversation.

That said, the traditional meaning — secrecy, spontaneity, and running away from disapproval — remains the most precise and historically accurate meaning. When you want to convey that element of secrecy or defiance, "elope" is the exact right word.

• It does not mean simply getting engaged.
  • It does not mean running away for any purpose other than marriage.
  • It does not mean having a small wedding that the family plans together and fully supports (though modern usage is slowly blurring this line).
  • It is not interchangeable with "divorce" or "break up" — it is always about getting married, never about ending a relationship.

To elope = to secretly run away with your partner to get married, usually without family knowledge or approval. The defining qualities are secrecy, evasion of family opposition, and the goal of immediate marriage. The word is inherently romantic in flavor, with a hint of rebellion.
